title: Vienna Game | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Against the Vienna, Nf6 is more accurate than Nc6.
White's passive d3 invites the principled reply — d5. Count the defenders: everything trades off, and that exchange on d5 favors Black. When White plays passively, strike the centre.
moves.teaches: Answer a passive setup by breaking in the centre where the exchanges work in your favor.

moves.spoken: Nc6, and resist taking on c3 — the doubled pawns don't really hurt White, and releasing the tension only strengthens his grip on the central squares.
moves.teaches: Don't inflict doubled pawns that actually reinforce the opponent's centre.

moves.spoken: More advanced isn't always better — Bg4 lets White set up the Nxe5 tactic. The dark bishop's primary job is simply to let you castle, so Be7 is perfect.
moves.teaches: Develop the dark-squared bishop to castle, not to the most forward square available.

moves.spoken: By the same logic Be6 reinforces the knight and stops Ng5 — bishops posted on safe, invulnerable squares.
moves.teaches: Place your pieces on unassailable squares that defend each other, not on ambitious but loose ones.

moves.spoken: a5 prevents b4 — if White got that in, b5 would follow and our e5-pawn could grow weak.
moves.teaches: A little a-pawn move can pre-empt an enemy pawn expansion that would loosen your centre.

moves.spoken: f6 stops Ng5 and shores up e5. When is f6 safe rather than weakening? Case by case — here White has no light bishop for that diagonal, so it weakens nothing.
moves.teaches: f6 is safe when the opponent can't exploit the diagonal it opens; judge it position by position.

moves.spoken: Now be concrete: h4 weakened g4, and the queen on d7 backs up a bishop there, while White's queen is off d1 so there's no Nxe5 trick. The very Bg4 I rejected earlier is now excellent — circumstances changed.
moves.teaches: A move that's bad in one position can be strong once the concrete factors around it change.

moves.spoken: Reinforce e5 with Bf6, not Bd6 which would drop the knight. Defend with the least valuable piece and keep your rooks free for bigger jobs.
moves.teaches: Accomplish a defensive task with your cheapest adequate piece; save the rooks and queen for real work.

moves.spoken: Rae8 completes the coordination — every piece is now working — and only then do we think about pressing with f4 or e4. No hurry.
moves.teaches: Finish coordinating all your pieces before you commit to the breakthrough.

moves.spoken: Now press the gas: f4 begins cracking White's kingside. It concedes the e4 square, but you can't make an omelet without breaking eggs — the attack is worth it.
moves.teaches: When your pieces are fully coordinated, launch the break even at the cost of a square.

moves.spoken: Don't fear retreating a long-range piece — the bishop on d8 eyes h4 exactly as it did from f6, and it clears the f-file for the rook. How far a move retreats says nothing about whether it's good.
moves.teaches: Retreat bishops and queens freely; long-range pieces attack just as well from behind and can unblock your own lines.

moves.spoken: Nf5 keeps the knight pressing the kingside, eyeing a Bxh4 sacrifice and a rook lift.
